Newborn Alaska hares emerge from the natal form with a body mass averaging approximately 100 grams [Wwb = approximately 100 grams], a relatively substantial neonatal weight that reflects the precocial developmental mode characteristic of leporids. This substantial birth mass allows the altricial neonate, termed a leveret, to achieve thermal independence and cursorial mobility within hours of parturition, a critical adaptation for evading predators in the open tundra habitats of western Alaska. The leveret's initial body mass, which is among the highest recorded for any North American lagomorph of similar adult size, provides a significant energy reserve that buffers against the nutritional unpredictability of early spring forage. Field studies have consistently documented that leverets born with a mass below this typical 100-gram [Wwb = typical 100-gram] threshold exhibit substantially reduced survival rates during the first two weeks, likely due to compromised thermoregulatory capacity and diminished competitive ability during suckling bouts.

After parturition, the nursing female establishes a pattern of infrequent but energetically rich provisioning bouts, a behavior that minimizes the risk of attracting mammalian predators to the natal form. The young begin nibbling solid vegetation remarkably early, and the transition to full nutritional independence is completed after approximately 23 days after birth [tx = approximately 23 days after birth], measured under the species' typical core body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This weaning period is notably brief for a mammal of this body size, reflecting the high metabolic demands and rapid growth trajectory that must be sustained during the short subarctic growing season. By the time the dam ceases lactation, the juvenile has typically tripled its birth mass and possesses a fully functional digestive system capable of processing the fibrous willow and graminoid shoots that constitute the adult diet. Individual variation in weaning age is influenced by maternal condition and local resource availability.

The gestation period for the Alaska hare, timed to coincide with the flush of new spring growth, lasts approximately 46 days [tg = approximately 46 days] when measured at the species' normothermic body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C]. This relatively brief intrauterine development period, which is consistent across most members of the genus Lepus, allows females to produce multiple litters within a single breeding season, thereby maximizing annual reproductive output in a highly seasonal environment. During gestation, the developing embryo undergoes rapid organogenesis, and the precocial neonates are delivered with their eyes open and a full coat of fur. The energetic cost of this accelerated development is substantial, requiring the gravid female to increase her daily food intake by an estimated 30 to 40 percent above maintenance levels. Data from captive studies indicate that the gestation length can vary by several days depending on maternal nutritional plane, though the 46-day (46 days) [tg = 46 days] figure represents the population mean at a temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C].

Females of the Alaska hare produce litters ranging from 4 to 8 pups per litter [N_R_i = 4 to 8 pups per litter], and under favorable conditions they may produce up to three such litters within a single breeding season [F_R_i = up to three such litters within a single breeding season]. This high fecundity is a classic life-history response to intense predation pressure, and it compensates for the relatively high first-year mortality rates observed in wild populations. The total reproductive output per female per year, which integrates both litter size and litter frequency, is among the highest reported for any arctic lagomorph and underscores the species' role as a key prey item for mammalian and avian predators. The energy required to sustain this reproductive effort is considerable, and females must sequester sufficient fat reserves during the brief summer to fuel both gestation and lactation. The maximum recorded annual reproductive rate for this species is estimated at 6 pups per 365 days, calculated at the reference body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], though actual output is often lower due to environmental constraints.

The Alaska hare exhibits a life-history schedule that is finely tuned to the extreme seasonality of its arctic and subarctic range. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonadal activity capable of producing viable gametes, is attained at approximately 266 days after birth [tp = approximately 266 days after birth], measured at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], meaning that individuals born early in the summer breeding season typically reach reproductive maturity by the following spring. The maximum lifespan documented in wild populations is about 18 years [am = about 18 years] at a body temperature of 39.7 °C [T = 39.7 °C], an exceptional longevity for a lagomorph that likely arises from the low metabolic scaling and the absence of significant senescence-related pathologies in predator-free environments. The ultimate adult wet weight for this species is approximately 4800 grams [Wwi = approximately 4800 grams], though exceptionally large individuals have been recorded at up to 7.2 kilograms, making the Alaska hare one of the largest extant leporids. This substantial body mass confers advantages in thermal inertia and predator defense, but it also imposes high absolute energetic demands that must be met through selective foraging on high-quality forage.
